impetuous

im-PECH-oo-uhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impetuous is acting or done suddenly, with little thought for the consequences.

His impetuous decision to skip the safety briefing nearly cost him his footing on the cliff trail.

Worked Example

Impetuous as ever, the young knight charged the enemy line alone before his captain could finish giving orders.

He acted the instant an impulse struck, without pausing to weigh the risk, which is the hallmark of impetuous behavior.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

impulsive: Impulsive means acting on a sudden inner urge without thinking it through -- buying, blurting, clicking before the thought arrives. Impetuous adds forceful, eager momentum: an impetuous act doesn't just skip the thinking, it charges ahead with hot energy. A quiet unplanned purchase is impulsive; storming out of a meeting is impetuous.

rash: Rash judges one particular decision by the risks it ignored -- a rash promise or a rash investment made with far too little caution. Impetuous describes the actor's manner instead: sudden, hot, swept along by impulse. We call the act rash when counting its dangers, impetuous when watching the person rush.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cautious: careful to avoid danger or mistakes

deliberate: done consciously and carefully, after consideration

Where it sits · how little the consequences are weighed — spontaneous → impetuous → reckless

spontaneous vs. impetuous: Spontaneous is weaker than impetuous: a spontaneous picnic is simply unplanned, while an impetuous decision goes further, rushing ahead with little thought for the consequences.

reckless vs. impetuous: Reckless is more extreme than impetuous: an impetuous act is hasty and thoughtless, but a reckless one goes further, ignoring obvious danger and safety altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — impetu

Root — impetu: a driving force or sudden impulse (from Latin impetus, 'an attack, force, impulse')

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of; full of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Impetuous is impetu ('a driving force or sudden impulse,' from Latin impetus) plus -ous, 'full of.' Someone impetuous is full of that sudden impulse, acting on it before stopping to think.

Use the root in a new word: impetus

Use the root in a new word: impetus: The coach's halftime speech provided the impetus the team needed to storm back in the second half.
